idCardOk.title: Your ID card or passport is enough
idCardOk.detail: For {{city}} a valid ID card or passport is enough. A provisional ID card (carte de identitate provizorie) is not valid for travel abroad.

idCardExtra.title: ID card accepted — passport recommended
idCardExtra.detail: Romanian citizens can usually enter with a valid ID card here, but a passport avoids problems at the border. Check MAE guidance for {{city}} before you go.

passportNeeded.title: Bring a passport
passportNeeded.detail: An ID card is not enough outside the EU/EEA. Check visa or entry-authorisation rules for {{city}} on the MAE site.

visaCheck.title: Check visa and entry rules
visaCheck.detail: Non-EU citizens may need a visa for {{city}}. Check the official rules for your nationality before booking.

ukEta.title: UK: passport + ETA
ukEta.detail: The UK does not accept EU ID cards. EU citizens need a passport and an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) approved before travel.

usEsta.title: USA: passport + ESTA or visa
usEsta.detail: You need a valid e-passport and either an approved ESTA (Visa Waiver Program) or a visa. Rules for Romanian citizens changed recently: confirm on the official site.

ees.title: EU Entry/Exit System (EES)
ees.detail: Non-EU travellers have fingerprints and a photo registered at the Schengen border. Allow extra time; ETIAS authorisation is expected to start later — check if it applies on your date.

validity.title: Check your document's expiry date
validity.detail: Your document must be valid for the whole trip. Many non-EU countries require a passport valid for 3–6 months after you arrive.

maeAlerts.title: Read the MAE travel alert
maeAlerts.detail: The Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs publishes entry rules and safety alerts for every country, including {{city}}.

childrenRo.title: Documents for children
childrenRo.detail: Each child needs their own ID card or passport. A child leaving Romania with only one parent, or with another adult, needs a notarised consent from the parent(s) who stay.

children.title: Documents for children
children.detail: Each child needs their own travel document. If a child travels without both parents, carry written consent from the absent parent.

liquids.title: Liquids: 100 ml rule
liquids.detail: In your cabin bag, liquids, gels and creams must be in containers of max 100 ml, all in one transparent resealable bag of about 1 litre. Some airports with new scanners allow more — only if the airport says so.

powerBank.title: Power banks and spare batteries: cabin only
powerBank.detail: Never put power banks or spare lithium batteries in checked baggage. Up to 100 Wh is fine; 100–160 Wh needs airline approval. Many airlines forbid using power banks during the flight.

sharp.title: No sharp or blunt items in the cabin
sharp.detail: Knives, scissors with blades longer than 6 cm, tools, bats and similar items must go in checked baggage or stay at home.

medication.title: Medication
medication.detail: Keep medicines in your cabin bag in their original packaging, with the prescription. Liquid medicines needed during the flight are exempt from the 100 ml rule — declare them at security.

babyFood.title: Baby food and milk
babyFood.detail: Baby food and milk needed during the trip are allowed over 100 ml. Security may ask you to open or test them.

cabinOnly.title: Check your cabin-bag size
cabinOnly.detail: Low-cost fares often include only a small under-seat bag (around 40 × 30 × 20 cm); a larger trolley costs extra. Check your airline's exact size and weight to avoid gate fees.

checkedBag.title: Checked bag paid and weighed?
checkedBag.detail: Make sure the checked bag is included in your booking. Adding it online before the flight is usually much cheaper than at the airport.

valuables.title: Valuables in the cabin
valuables.detail: Keep documents, money, keys, medicines and electronics in your cabin bag, not in the checked one.

weigh.title: Weigh your bags at home
weigh.detail: A luggage scale avoids surprises at the airport, where overweight fees are high.

renewEarly.title: Passport: act now if needed
renewEarly.detail: {{days}} days to go. If your passport is missing or expires soon, apply now; for urgent trips a temporary passport can be issued faster.

onlineCheckin.title: Check in online
onlineCheckin.detail: Many airlines open online check-in 24–48 hours before departure. Low-cost airlines may charge for check-in at the airport.

arriveEarly.title: Be at the airport {{hours}} h before
arriveEarly.detail: Recommended for this flight, to leave time for check-in, security and passport control. Bag drop and gates close earlier than departure.

boardingPass.title: Boarding pass ready
boardingPass.detail: Keep the boarding pass in the airline app or printed, plus a screenshot in case you have no signal.

cash.title: Cash of €10,000 or more must be declared
cash.detail: When you enter or leave the EU carrying €10,000 or more (or the equivalent), you must declare it to customs.

meatDairy.title: No meat or dairy products into the EU
meatDairy.detail: You cannot bring meat, milk or products made from them into the EU from most non-EU countries, even sandwiches.

allowances.title: Duty-free allowances
allowances.detail: Arriving in the EU by air you can bring, tax-free, e.g. 200 cigarettes, 1 L of spirits, 4 L of wine and other goods up to €430. Above that, declare them.

eu261.title: EU passenger rights apply
eu261.detail: Your flight departs from the EU, so Regulation 261/2004 applies: for long delays, cancellations or denied boarding you may get care and €250–600 compensation.

eu261Inbound.title: EU rights: depends on the airline
eu261Inbound.detail: Flights into the EU are covered by Regulation 261/2004 only if the airline is an EU airline. Keep receipts and the boarding pass if something goes wrong.

pet_eu.title: Pet in the EU: pet passport, microchip, rabies vaccine
pet_eu.detail: Dogs, cats and ferrets need an EU pet passport, a microchip (put in before the vaccine) and a valid rabies vaccine given at least 21 days before travel. Finland, Ireland, Malta and Norway also require a tapeworm treatment for dogs. Other animals follow the destination's national rules.

pet_intoEu.title: Pet entering the EU: health certificate
pet_intoEu.detail: Coming from outside the EU, a dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, a valid rabies vaccine and an EU animal health certificate signed by an official vet (valid 10 days until the border check). From many countries a rabies blood test (at least 0.5 IU/ml) is also needed, taken at least 90 days before the certificate. Returning with a valid EU pet passport is simpler.

pet_gb.title: Pet to Great Britain: only as cargo
pet_gb.detail: Pets flying into Great Britain must travel as cargo with an approved airline or company, not in the cabin or as checked baggage. Only recognised guide and assistance dogs may fly in the cabin. The pet needs a microchip, a rabies vaccine and a health certificate or pet passport; dogs also need a tapeworm treatment.

pet_us.title: Dog to the USA: CDC Dog Import Form
pet_us.detail: Since 1 August 2024 every dog must be at least 6 months old, microchipped, healthy and have a CDC Dog Import Form receipt. Dogs that were in high-risk rabies countries in the last 6 months need extra documents. Airlines and US states may ask for more.

pet_usCats.title: Cats to the USA
pet_usCats.detail: Cats have their own CDC rules (the dog form does not apply); the airline or the US state may ask for a health certificate or rabies vaccine.

pet_tr.title: Pet to Türkiye
pet_tr.detail: Türkiye asks for a microchip, a rabies vaccine, a rabies blood test (above 0.5 IU/ml, at least 30 days after the vaccine and 90 days before entry) and a vet health certificate. At most 2 animals per passenger.

pet_ae.title: Pet to the UAE: import permit
pet_ae.detail: You need an import permit from the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (valid 90 days), a microchip, a rabies vaccine and a certified vet health certificate; the pet is checked on arrival.

pet_other.title: Pet: check {{city}}'s rules
pet_other.detail: Every non-EU country has its own rules for pets (microchip, vaccines, blood tests, permits, quarantine). Ask that country's embassy or veterinary authority before booking; the MAE page lists entry rules by country.

petAirlineUnknown.title: Your airline decides if the pet can fly
petAirlineUnknown.detail: Airlines differ a lot: Wizz Air, Ryanair and easyJet do not carry pets at all, while many others take a small pet in the cabin (usually up to 8 kg with the carrier). Fill in your airline to see its exact rules.

petAirlineNo.title: {{airline}} does not carry pets
petAirlineNo.detail: {{airline}} does not take pets in the cabin or in the hold; only recognised assistance dogs may fly. Choose another airline for your pet.

petAirlineCabin.title: Book the pet with {{airline}} in advance
petAirlineCabin.detail: {{airline}} takes a small pet in the cabin (up to {{kg}} kg with the carrier). Places are limited, so add the pet to your booking as early as possible and wait for confirmation.

petAirlineGb.title: Pet to Great Britain with {{airline}}
petAirlineGb.detail: Even if {{airline}} normally takes pets in the cabin, pets flying into Great Britain must travel as cargo. Arrange it with an approved pet transport company.

petAirlineCargo.title: {{airline}}: pets only as cargo
petAirlineCargo.detail: {{airline}} does not take pets in the cabin; they travel in the hold through its cargo partner. Ask for a quote well in advance.

step.none: Less than 2 hours of difference: keep your normal schedule, drink water and rest well the night before.
step.flight: On board: set your watch to destination time. Sleep if it is night there, stay awake if it is day. Drink water, skip alcohol.
step.light_east: After landing: get outdoor light in the morning and avoid bright light and screens in the evening.
step.light_west: After landing: get outdoor light in the afternoon and evening; keep mornings dim for the first days.
step.caffeine: Coffee only in the local morning, none in the 8 hours before bedtime. A short nap (under 30 min) is fine; long naps delay adjustment.

arrive.title: Arrive at the departures hall
arrive.detail: Be there {{hours}} h before departure, with your ID or passport and boarding pass ready.

checkin.title: Drop your checked bag
checkin.detail: Find your airline's desk on the departure screens. Bag drop usually closes 40–60 minutes before departure; your booking has the exact time.

security.title: Security check
security.detail: Liquids up to 100 ml in one clear 1-litre bag, laptop and power banks out, nothing sharp.

passportOut.title: Passport control
passportOut.detail: Your flight leaves the Schengen area, so a border officer checks your passport or ID before the gates.

gate.title: Go to your gate
gate.detail: The gate appears on the departure screens. Boarding usually closes 15–30 minutes before departure.

passportIn.title: Passport control
passportIn.detail: Your flight comes from outside the Schengen area: queue for the border check with your passport or ID.

baggage.title: Collect your checked bag
baggage.detail: Look for your flight number on the baggage-claim screens to find the right belt.

customs.title: Customs
customs.detail: Your flight crosses the EU border: take the green channel if you have nothing to declare, the red one if you do (for example €10,000 or more in cash).

exit.title: Exit and transport to {{city}}
exit.detail: Follow the exit signs; trains, buses and taxis are marked on the map.

help.disclaimer: Flywell gives general first-aid tips, not a diagnosis. If you feel seriously unwell, press the call button and tell the crew straight away.

breathe.title: Breathe with me
breathe.intro: Follow the circle. Breathe in through your nose, breathe out slowly through your mouth.
breathe.ground: Name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell and 1 you can taste. Turbulence feels strong, but planes are built for it.

crew.title: Show this to the crew
crew.callButton: Press the call button above your seat (the person symbol), then show this screen to the flight attendant.
crew.addCard: Add allergies and medication to this card

unwell.title: I feel unwell
unwell.urgentTitle: Call the crew now if you have
unwell.urgent: chest pain, trouble breathing, swelling of the face or lips, fainting, weakness on one side, confusion or heavy bleeding. If you carry your own adrenaline pen or inhaler, use it as prescribed.

panic.title: Panic or fear of flying
steps: Breathe slowly: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 6.
Press your feet into the floor and relax your shoulders.
Tell the crew you are anxious; they help nervous flyers every day.

nausea.title: Nausea or motion sickness
steps: Look at a fixed point and keep your head still.
Open the air vent above you and loosen tight clothing.
Sip water in small amounts; the sick bag is in the seat pocket.

ears.title: Ear pain or pressure
steps: Swallow, yawn or chew gum, especially during descent.
Gently pinch your nose, close your mouth and blow softly.
Babies: feed them or give a dummy during take-off and landing.

faint.title: Dizzy or about to faint
steps: Sit back, loosen your belt and lower your head if you can.
Drink water and eat something sweet if you have it.
Tell the crew; do not stand up quickly or walk alone.

headache.title: Headache or dehydration
steps: Drink a glass of water every hour; cabin air is very dry.
Skip alcohol and extra coffee on the flight.
Take only medicine you already know you can use.

turbulence.title: Scared of turbulence
steps: Keep your seatbelt fastened; turbulence is uncomfortable but normal.
Breathe out slowly and let your body move with the seat.
Listen to the crew: if they keep serving, all is routine.

seats.title: The right seat for you
seats.subtitle: Pick your situation and the plane shows where to aim and what to avoid. Rows differ between aircraft, so match them to your airline's seat map.

summary.child: Over the wing or just in front of it, window and middle seats together, away from exit rows and the last rows.
summary.turbulence: Rows over the wing feel the least turbulence; the last rows feel the most.
summary.fear: Sit over the wing, on the aisle, and tell the crew you are nervous — they are used to it.
summary.motion: A window seat over the wing, where the ride is smoothest.
summary.legroom: Exit rows or the first row have the most space.
summary.quickExit: An aisle seat in the first rows gets you off first.
summary.sleep: A window seat away from the toilets and galleys.
summary.mobility: An aisle seat near the front, not in an exit row, with assistance booked ahead.

child.1: Put a child seat by the window: it must not block the way out of the row. Ask the airline which child seats it accepts.
child.2: Children and infants cannot sit in exit rows — the crew will move you.
child.3: The back of the cabin bumps the most, and people queue there for the toilets, so stay over the wing or further forward.

turbulence.1: Over the wing is closest to the plane's centre of gravity, so movement is smallest; the tail moves the most.
turbulence.2: Keep your seat belt loosely fastened all flight — turbulence can happen in clear sky.

fear.1: Over the wing the ride is smoothest and the engine sound stays steady.
fear.2: An aisle seat helps if you feel closed in; a window helps if seeing the horizon calms you.
fear.3: Tap Help in the During the flight tab of your trip for a breathing exercise that works in airplane mode.

motion.1: Look at the horizon and keep your head still against the headrest.
motion.2: Avoid reading during take-off and bumpy parts, and point the air vent at your face.

legroom.1: Exit rows are only for adults able and willing to help open the exit; the crew may move you if you are not suitable.
legroom.2: The first row has extra room but no space under the seat in front for bags during take-off and landing.

quickExit.1: Front rows on the aisle are best for tight connections.
quickExit.2: In an emergency the distance to a usable exit matters most: when you sit down, count the rows to the exits in front of and behind you.

sleep.1: A window gives you something to lean on and nobody climbs over you.
sleep.2: The front and back of the cabin have toilets and galleys: light, noise and queues.

mobility.1: Ask your airline for free assistance at least 48 hours before the flight — EU rules give you this right.
mobility.2: Some aisle seats have armrests that lift, which makes moving across easier; ask when you book.

seats.comfortOnly: Comfort tip — there is no safety data behind it.
seats.aircraftNote: Drawn on a typical 30-row plane (A320 / Boeing 737). Wing and exit rows differ on your aircraft; check the seat map when you choose your seat.

tips: Keep your seat belt fastened whenever you are seated.
Drink water regularly and go easy on alcohol and coffee.
Stand up, stretch and move your ankles every hour or two.
On descent, swallow, yawn or chew to ease the pressure in your ears.
